title: Seen: Hanuman's first word
hookLine: Hanuman has the biggest news of Rama's life, and he chooses his first word with care
carry: vak tapas: speech that's true, kind and calming

cards: Rama has been waiting on a mountain outside Kishkindha. The search parties from the north, the east and the west have already come back with nothing.

Now the southern party arrives, loud and happy, and Hanuman steps forward. He has crossed the sea, found her, spoken with her, fought half of Lanka and left it burning. He has a long, astonishing story to tell.
And first he has to decide which word comes out of his mouth.

teach.b: The word he puts first, in Valmiki's Sanskrit, is drishta. Seen. He bows and tells Rama the queen has been seen, that she is keeping her vows, that she is unharmed.
Think about the order. If he had begun with the ocean, or Lanka, or the words I went, Rama would have spent every sentence waiting, heart in his throat.
If he had begun with her name alone, Rama might have braced for the worst.
Seen comes first, and the fear is answered before it can rise.
The Tamil poet Kamban, retelling the story, makes it even sharper: his Hanuman opens with the Tamil for I saw, before he names her at all.
Only then does Hanuman tell the rest: the leap, the city at night, the ashoka grove, a thin woman under a tree, Ravana's threats, Rama's own ring passed down through the branches.
Joy comes over Rama and Lakshmana as they listen. Sugriva had already guessed, from the monkeys' wild celebration on the way home. Hindus have a name for this kind of care.

teach.h: VAK TAPAS: THE DISCIPLINE OF SPEECH.
teach.b: The Bhagavad Gita calls it the tapas, the discipline, of speech: words that are true, kind and helpful, and that don't stir up fear. Speech is part of your spiritual practice, not just your manners.
And Hanuman is its great example. When Rama first met him in the forest, he told Lakshmana he'd never heard anyone speak so well.
Here, with the biggest news of Rama's life, Hanuman proves it: before he speaks, he thinks about where his words will land.

how: Ramayana teachers, in temples and in family readings, often pause on Hanuman's first word, seen, as a lesson in the Gita's discipline of speech; Kamban's Tamil Ramayana gives the same moment as I saw.

games.q: you're Hanuman, back from Lanka with the biggest news of Rama's life. what do you say first?
o: the whole story, from the leap.
games.why: Valmiki's Hanuman opens with seen, drishta, so the fear is answered before anything else is said. that's vak tapas: true words, placed with care.

practice: Many Hindus keep mauna, a short stretch of silence, as part of their practice. Sit in mauna now for a few breaths.

Then think of one piece of news you'll bring someone soon, and try the Gita's test: is it true, is it kind, does it help, will it ease their fear rather than raise it? Find the first word that answers their fear.
If you pray, offer your words before you speak them.

wordCard.voice: Seen. Drishta in Sanskrit. Hanuman's first word to Rama, put first on purpose, so the fear is over before the story begins.

orig.note: Sanskrit dṛṣṭā: seen, the past participle of dṛś, to see; here in the feminine, agreeing with Sita.

carryVoice: Your line: vak tapas, speech that's true, kind and calming. Tomorrow, what he carried back in his hand. Day six hundred thirty-two, done.
